pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Waves & How They Move

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum — KS3 Physics, bridged):** England introduces the formal wave model — amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and transverse vs longitudinal waves — at Key Stage 3 (Physics: 'Waves'), not in KS2. At age 9–10 this record is an early bridge to that KS3 content, building the amplitude/wavelength vocabulary and the energy-transfer idea on concrete media before the quantitative treatment (v = fλ) at KS3/KS4.

- **Standards — US (NGSS 4-PS4-1):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-1]." (Clarification limits this to standard, repeating waves; the assessment boundary excludes interference, electromagnetic waves, non-periodic/non-uniform waves, and any quantitative model.) This is the anchoring standard for the topic.

- **Operational details:** Children build a first MODEL of a wave: amplitude = the height/size of the wave (bigger amplitude carries more energy, so it moves objects more), and wavelength = the distance from one peak to the next. Develop it on concrete media — a slinky, a rope, water in a tray/ripple tank — observing and describing before naming the quantities on a drawn transverse waveform (crest, trough, amplitude, wavelength). The threshold idea to secure is that a wave transfers ENERGY, not matter: a cork or bead floating on water bobs up and down in place while the wave travels on through it; a ribbon tied to a slinky oscillates but does not travel along the coil. Use the domino / Mexican-wave analogy for energy passed neighbour-to-neighbour, and demonstrate that waves DO work — a bigger-amplitude wave pushes a floating object more — which ties directly back to the volume–amplitude prerequisite from sound.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). The child can label amplitude and wavelength on a wave, model wave patterns on a slinky/rope/water and describe them, relate larger amplitude to more energy (moves objects more), and — the key threshold — explain that the medium bobs in place while only energy travels through it. Mastery is a qualitative, correctly-modelled wave with the energy-not-matter idea held; the wave equation and transverse/longitudinal formalism are deferred (Tier C, KS3).
bestPractices: Develop the model on concrete media first — slinky, rope, water tray/ripple tank — observing and describing wave patterns before naming the quantities.

Introduce amplitude = height/size of the wave (linked to energy: bigger amplitude moves objects more) and wavelength = distance between successive peaks, anchored on a drawn transverse waveform (crest, trough).

Directly confront the energy-not-matter misconception with a floating cork/bead (bobs in place) or a ribbon on a slinky (oscillates but doesn't travel along) — the observable evidence that matter is left behind.
Use the falling-dominoes and stadium 'Mexican wave' analogies for energy passed neighbour-to-neighbour while each particle stays roughly in place.
Demonstrate that waves do WORK — a bigger-amplitude wave pushes a floating object more — connecting amplitude–energy back to the sound volume–vibration-size prerequisite.
Have children label crest, trough, amplitude and wavelength on their own diagrams, and distinguish amplitude (how tall) from wavelength (how long) explicitly.
keyRepresentations: Slinky or rope pulse — a coil oscillates but does not travel the length of the spring (energy transmitted, not mass).
Water ripple tank with a floating cork/buoy that bobs up and down in place as waves pass.
Labelled transverse waveform — crest, trough, amplitude as height, wavelength as peak-to-peak distance.
Falling-dominoes / stadium Mexican-wave analogy for neighbour-to-neighbour energy transfer.
commonMisconceptions: Believing waves carry MATTER along with them (the water or cork travels to the shore) rather than the medium bobbing in place while only energy travels through — the central wave misconception.
Confusing amplitude with wavelength (mixing up 'how tall' with 'how long').
Thinking a bigger (higher-amplitude) wave automatically travels faster — wave speed depends on the medium, not the amplitude.
Reading a drawn sine curve as the literal path an object or a sound takes (sound is actually longitudinal).
Treating 'energy' as a substance/stuff that flows along, reinforced if 'energy travels' is taught carelessly.

learn.summary: For ages 9–10, build a first qualitative model of waves: amplitude (the height/size of a wave from the middle line to a peak) and wavelength (the distance from one peak to the next), plus the threshold idea that a wave transfers energy, not matter. Develop the model on concrete media (slinky, rope, water in a tray or ripple tank) by observing and describing before naming the quantities on a drawn transverse waveform. The central misconception to confront is that waves carry matter along; for a standard repeating wave a floating cork or duck bobs roughly in place while only the wave pattern (energy) travels through. Keep the treatment qualitative: the wave equation (v = fλ) and the transverse/longitudinal formalism are deferred to later study. Amplitude links energy to a visible effect (bigger-amplitude waves push floating objects more), connecting back to the sound idea that louder means a bigger vibration; wave speed, by contrast, is set by the medium, not the amplitude.

activities.title: Does the cork ride the wave? (water-tray investigation)
feedback: If the learner predicted the cork rides to the far end: watch again closely — the cork bobs up and down and ends up near where it started, even though wave after wave passes under it. What crossed the tray was the wave pattern (energy), not the water itself.

If the learner says the water travelled across: a single bit of water moves round in a small loop (up and down and a little back and forth) and stays roughly in place; the pattern moves across, the water does not travel with it.
Reinforce correct observation: the cork stayed roughly put and bobbed — so the wave carries energy, not matter, across the tray.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain task on real water directly surfaces and tests the central wave misconception (matter travels with the wave). Watching the cork stay put while waves pass provides observable evidence that it is energy, not matter, that crosses. (In a small tray a very large disturbance can produce some visible drift; keep disturbances modest so the bob-in-place behaviour is clear.)
sourceClaims: Classical waves transfer energy without transporting matter through the medium: waves in a pond do not carry water molecules along; the wave's energy travels through the water leaving the molecules in place, like a bug bobbing on ripples. Mechanical waves pass energy molecule to molecule like falling dominoes. Wavelength is the distance between crests.

A common misconception is that matter travels with a wave; in fact particles move back and forth (perpendicular to the wave's travel) and take part by bumping into one another and passing on energy, so the average particle position does not change. Useful teaching analogies: a bobbing buoy and the stadium 'Mexican wave'.
learnerActions: Float a cork or bottle-top on one end of a tray of water.
Before making any waves, predict in writing or speech: will the cork travel to the far end with the waves, or do something else — and why?
Make waves from one end and watch the cork carefully as several waves pass under it.
Describe what actually crossed the tray: did the water (and cork) travel across, or did the cork stay roughly in place and bob up and down?
Repeat with a bigger disturbance and note whether the cork is now carried across or just bobs more strongly in roughly the same place.
activities.intendedInsight: A wave transfers energy through a medium without carrying the matter along: the cork bobs up and down roughly in place while the wave pattern sweeps on through it.

activities.title: Pass it along: slinky, rope, and the stadium wave
feedback: If the learner thinks the ribbon travels along the coil: it returns to roughly its own spot — only the pulse travels the length, showing matter stays put while the wave (energy) moves.

If the learner predicts the big pulse arrives first: on the same slinky the big and small pulses reach the far end at about the same time; amplitude carries more energy, not more speed. Wave speed is set by the medium, not the size of the wave.

For the stadium/domino analogy: no single person travels round the stadium and no single domino moves along the row — each only moves and nudges its neighbour, so what travels round is the wave (energy), not the people or dominoes.
activities.rationale: The slinky/rope makes energy-not-matter directly observable and lets a same-speed comparison confront the 'bigger wave travels faster' misconception. The domino and Mexican-wave analogies make neighbour-to-neighbour energy transfer concrete.
sourceClaims: A common misconception is that matter travels with a wave; in fact particles move back and forth (perpendicular to the wave's travel) and take part by bumping into one another and passing on energy, so the average particle position does not change. Useful teaching analogies: a bobbing buoy and the stadium 'Mexican wave'.

Classical waves transfer energy without transporting matter through the medium: waves in a pond do not carry water molecules along; the wave's energy travels through the water leaving the molecules in place, like a bug bobbing on ripples. Mechanical waves pass energy molecule to molecule like falling dominoes. Wavelength is the distance between crests.
learnerActions: Lay a slinky or long rope on the floor and send a single pulse from one end to the other; watch the far end react.
Tie a ribbon or marker near the middle of the coil and watch what the ribbon does as the pulse passes it.
Describe what the ribbon does (oscillates and returns to roughly its own spot) versus what the pulse does (travels the length).
Send a big pulse and a small pulse and compare how fast each reaches the far end.
Act out or describe a stadium 'Mexican wave' or a line of falling dominoes, then say which individuals actually travel round/along and which only pass the motion to their neighbour.
activities.intendedInsight: Energy is passed neighbour-to-neighbour while each part of the medium stays roughly in place; for ordinary-sized pulses, the size of a pulse makes little or no difference to how fast it travels along a given medium.

activities.title: Label the wave: amplitude vs wavelength
feedback: If amplitude is marked as the peak-to-peak distance: that distance is the wavelength; amplitude is the height from the middle line up to a peak.
If wavelength is marked as the height: that height is the amplitude; wavelength is measured from one peak across to the next peak.
When both are labelled correctly and the two 'change one at a time' drawings differ as expected, confirm: the learner has separated how tall a wave is from how long it is.
activities.rationale: Explicitly labelling on the learner's own diagram and drawing waves that vary one quantity at a time targets the amplitude/wavelength confusion directly and builds the vocabulary the later formal model depends on.

Classical waves transfer energy without transporting matter through the medium: waves in a pond do not carry water molecules along; the wave's energy travels through the water leaving the molecules in place, like a bug bobbing on ripples. Mechanical waves pass energy molecule to molecule like falling dominoes. Wavelength is the distance between crests.
learnerActions: Draw (or be given) a transverse waveform and mark the crest (highest point) and trough (lowest point).
Mark amplitude as the height from the middle line to a peak, and label it 'how big / how much energy'.
Mark wavelength as the distance from one peak to the next peak, and label it 'how long'.
State in your own words the difference between amplitude (how tall) and wavelength (how long).
Draw a second wave with the same wavelength but larger amplitude, and a third with the same amplitude but longer wavelength, to show the two quantities change independently.
activities.intendedInsight: Amplitude and wavelength are two separate, independent features of a wave: amplitude is the height (linked to energy), wavelength is the peak-to-peak distance.

activities.title: Bigger wave, bigger push: amplitude and energy
feedback: If the learner attributes the bigger push to higher speed: recall the slinky — big and small pulses travelled at the same speed. The bigger push comes from more energy (larger amplitude), not greater speed.
Reinforce the sound link: just as a louder note is a bigger vibration, a bigger water wave is a bigger disturbance carrying more energy.
Confirm correct reasoning: bigger amplitude = more energy = bigger effect on the floating object, with speed set by the medium.
activities.rationale: Demonstrating that waves do work ties the amplitude–energy idea to a visible effect and reconnects to the sound volume–vibration-size prerequisite, while the same-speed result guards against conflating amplitude with speed.
sourceClaims: NGSS 4-PS4-1: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-1]; clarification limits to standard repeating waves and the boundary excludes interference, EM waves, non-periodic waves and quantitative models.
learnerActions: Float a small object (toy boat, bottle-top) on a water tray and make a small-amplitude wave, noting how much the object is pushed or bobs.
Make a bigger-amplitude wave (same medium) and compare how much the object is pushed or bobs now.
State the relationship: a bigger-amplitude wave carries more energy and moves the object more.
Connect to sound: louder sound comes from a bigger vibration (bigger amplitude), just as a bigger water wave is a bigger disturbance carrying more energy.
Decide and explain whether a bigger wave moves the object more because it travels faster or because it carries more energy — and justify using the slinky same-speed result.
activities.intendedInsight: Larger amplitude means more energy, which does more work on objects (a bigger push), but it does not make the wave travel faster.

activities.title: Optional: side-on wave model with amplitude and wavelength controls
feedback: If the learner expects the cork to ride to the far side: the model shows it bobbing in place and left behind — the pattern travels, the cork does not.
When amplitude is raised and the push grows but the crossing time does not shorten, confirm: amplitude sets energy/push, not speed.
If amplitude and wavelength are confused on the labels, point to which control changed height versus peak spacing.
activities.rationale: A manipulable side-on model makes the two independent quantities and the energy-not-matter behaviour visible together; live labels and linked recolouring of crest/trough and a pushed boat make the mechanism concrete. This is offered as an optional complement to the hands-on media, not a replacement for real investigation; its smooth surface and marked particle are an idealised model of a real wave.

A common misconception is that matter travels with a wave; in fact particles move back and forth (perpendicular to the wave's travel) and take part by bumping into one another and passing on energy, so the average particle position does not change. Useful teaching analogies: a bobbing buoy and the stadium 'Mexican wave'.
learnerActions: Use a side-on model of a rope or water wave with two separate controls: one that raises the amplitude (a taller wave) and one that stretches the wavelength (peaks further apart), with the terms shown live on the crest and trough as they change.
Predict where a floating cork on the surface will end up, then send a wave across and watch: the cork bobs straight up and down and is left near its starting point while the pattern sweeps through.
Increase the amplitude and observe the same cork bob higher and a floating boat rock and bob more strongly, while both still stay near their starting points — bigger wave, more energy, bigger effect.
Compare a tall wave and a short wave sent across and note whether changing amplitude changed how fast the wave crossed.
activities.intendedInsight: Amplitude and wavelength can be varied independently, and a wave carries energy (which can push objects) without carrying the floating object along with it.

activities.title: Check and consolidate the wave model
feedback: If the learner says the duck is carried to the far bank: revisit the cork/slinky evidence — for a standard repeating wave the medium bobs in place while energy crosses.

If waves are ordered by wavelength instead of amplitude when ranking energy: for these same-wavelength waves, the difference in energy comes from amplitude (height), so compare heights, not peak spacing.
If the learner reads the curve as the route the water follows: the curve is a graph of displacement; a marked particle actually moves up and down (or back and forth), not along the wavy line.
Confirm a full response: duck bobs in place, energy crosses, amplitude is distinguished from wavelength, and amplitude does not set speed.
activities.rationale: A focused set of recognition and short-explanation checks consolidates the model and re-tests each misconception; recognition-style items confirm vocabulary but do not by themselves elicit the independent, hands-on observation that overturns the matter-travels misconception, so they should follow the investigations rather than replace them.

A common misconception is that matter travels with a wave; in fact particles move back and forth (perpendicular to the wave's travel) and take part by bumping into one another and passing on energy, so the average particle position does not change. Useful teaching analogies: a bobbing buoy and the stadium 'Mexican wave'.
learnerActions: Label amplitude, wavelength, crest and trough on a given waveform.
Answer: as a standard, repeating wave crosses a pond toward the far bank, does a floating duck get carried to the bank, or bob in place? Justify the answer.
Order several drawn waves that have the same wavelength (in the same medium) by the energy they carry, using their amplitudes.
Explain, using a marked particle, why the drawn wavy curve is NOT the path the water or duck physically travels.
Write one or two sentences summarising what a wave carries across (energy) versus what stays behind (the matter/medium).
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the vocabulary (amplitude, wavelength, crest, trough), the energy-from-amplitude ordering, and the energy-not-matter threshold idea, including why a drawn sine curve is a displacement graph rather than a travel path.

constraints: Keep the treatment qualitative at this age: the wave equation (v = fλ) and the transverse/longitudinal formalism are deferred to later study (KS3/KS4).
Scope to standard, repeating waves; exclude interference, electromagnetic waves, non-periodic/non-uniform waves and any quantitative model (per the NGSS 4-PS4-1 assessment boundary).
The central threshold to secure is energy-not-matter: ensure learners observe the medium bobbing in place, not merely hear it stated.
Distinguish the drawn sine curve (a displacement graph) from the actual motion of a particle (up and down, or back and forth); do not let learners treat the curve as a travel path.
Amplitude is linked to energy and to how much a wave moves objects, not to wave speed; wave speed is set by the medium. Any example comparing wave sizes should keep speed constant.
Recognition/labelling checks confirm vocabulary but do not elicit the independent hands-on observation; use them after, not instead of, concrete investigation on slinky/rope/water.
A side-on screen model is an idealised representation; use it alongside, not in place of, real media, and treat its smooth surface and marked particle as a model of the real wave.
A paper waveform diagram represents an ideal wave shape; keep learners aware it is a graph, not a photograph of moving water.
Tie amplitude–energy explicitly back to the sound prerequisite (louder = bigger vibration) so the two topics reinforce one another.

The bob-in-place answer applies to the idealised standard repeating wave; frame learner prompts around a pond/tray crossing rather than a breaking shoreline, where wind and surf can drift objects inshore (outside this objective's scope).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row marked two citations (Science Learning Hub; DfE National Curriculum) as verified:false; confidence in those claims should be treated accordingly and re-checked before relying on them. Activity 1's energy-not-matter principle is independently supported by the verified:true NASA claim.

Self-audit: the original 'bigger wave travels faster' is a listed misconception and is correctly treated as wrong in the activities (wave speed depends on the medium, not amplitude); the big/small pulse same-speed comparison is used to confront it.

Self-audit on energy language: 'energy/the wave pattern travels' is used, but the row warns that treating energy as a flowing substance can reinforce a misconception. Activities frame energy as what is transferred/passed neighbour-to-neighbour while matter stays in place, rather than a stuff that physically flows along.

The claim that water-wave particles trace small circular orbits is accurate for deep-water surface waves but is beyond this Tier-B objective and is intentionally not taught; mentioned only as a note on why a 3D view was considered.

The original strongly asserted a coded interactive is 'ideal' and that a quiz 'only assesses' / a static image 'cannot show' the dynamic behaviour; these comparative-efficacy claims are not established by the sources and have been softened to scoped affordances and limits.

The consolidation 'shore/beach' wording was reframed to a pond/far-bank crossing: at a real breaking shoreline, wind and surf can genuinely carry a floating object inshore, which conflicts with the idealised bob-in-place answer and is outside the standard-repeating-wave scope.
Activity 1's sourceClaims were trimmed to drop the NGSS 4-PS4-1 claim, which supports the general model/topic but not the specific energy-not-matter principle that activity teaches.

Independent re-audit confirmation: physics claims, initial conditions and amplitude/speed/energy logic were re-checked occurrence-by-occurrence and found consistent; no new learner-facing errors identified. Whether a classroom water tray reliably shows a clean amplitude-dependent push without visible drift remains setup-dependent and unverified.

assess.poeTask: Float a cork or bottle-top on a tray of water and make waves from one end. Predict: will the cork travel to the far end with the waves, or do something else? Say why first, then make the waves and explain what actually crossed the tray.
probeDeeper: On a slinky you send a big pulse and a small pulse together — which reaches the far end first, or do they arrive together? What does that tell you about speed and size?
When a Mexican wave goes round a stadium, does any single person travel round the stadium? So what actually moves round?
You said this wave is bigger — does that mean it carries more energy, or moves faster, or both?
assess.correctAnswer: The duck bobs up and down mostly in place as each wave passes under it — it is NOT carried along to the far bank. The wave transfers ENERGY across the pond; the water (and the duck) stay roughly where they are, just moving up and down.

errorPatterns.pattern: Matter travels with the wave: 'the duck rides the wave to the far bank' — the water moves bodily across
errorPatterns.nextMove: Float a cork and watch it bob in PLACE while the wave passes through; the wave moves, the water doesn't travel with it — energy is what crosses.
errorPatterns.distractor: The duck is carried across to the far bank by the waves.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the duck is carried along in the direction the wave travels

errorPatterns.pattern: Amplitude and wavelength confused: mixes up the height of the wave with the distance between peaks
errorPatterns.nextMove: Amplitude = height from the middle to a peak (how big/energetic); wavelength = distance from one peak to the next; label both on a marked diagram.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels amplitude as the peak-to-peak distance, or wavelength as the height

errorPatterns.pattern: Bigger wave = faster: 'a taller wave must travel across faster'
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a slinky, a big pulse and a small pulse travel at the SAME speed (set by the medium); amplitude carries more energy, not more speed.
errorPatterns.distractor: A bigger (taller) wave travels across faster than a small one.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts a bigger-amplitude wave moves across the pond faster than a small one

errorPatterns.pattern: Sine curve as a literal path: reads the drawn wave shape as the route a particle physically follows
errorPatterns.nextMove: The curve is a graph of displacement; a marked particle actually moves straight up and down (or back and forth), not along the curve.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the water or duck moves ALONG the wavy line drawn on paper

responseLevels.gap: Says the duck/water is carried along in the direction of travel (matter travels with the wave), or reads the wave curve as a physical path.
responseLevels.full: Explains the duck bobs in place while ENERGY is transferred across, distinguishes amplitude (height/energy) from wavelength (peak spacing), holds that amplitude doesn't set speed, and transfers to the Mexican-wave and slinky cases.
responseLevels.partial: Knows waves have amplitude and wavelength and that bigger waves carry more energy, but still thinks the medium (duck/water) travels along with the wave, or confuses amplitude with wavelength.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A duck floats on a pond. Waves travel across the pond from left to right and pass under the duck. Does the duck get carried along to the right-hand bank by the waves, or does it do something else? Explain what the waves actually carry across the pond.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Everyone has 'seen' waves carry things to shore, so the intuitive answer is the duck rides along. Asking what actually crosses the pond forces the energy-not-matter distinction. A child with the threshold idea says the duck bobs in place while the wave carries energy; the misconception child has the duck transported. This is the single central wave misconception at every age.
